title: (Scenario) PostgreSQL is approaching its write capacity — what would you do BEFORE sharding (establish which resource is actually at its limit — CPU, lock contention, connection pressure, WAL generation, a handful of expensive queries — then examine query/index design, transaction duration, unnecessary writes, batching, connection behavior, data lifecycle, vertical headroom, and workload separation, because sharding changes application development permanently)?
shortTitle: PostgreSQL is approaching its write capacity — what would you do before sharding?

s1_definition.profdef: Sharding — horizontally partitioning data across multiple independent database instances — is the most expensive and least reversible scaling step, because it permanently changes how the application queries data: cross-shard joins, transactions, and unique constraints become hard or impossible, and every query must carry or derive a shard key. Before sharding you first diagnose which specific resource is actually saturated (CPU, lock contention, connection pressure, write-ahead-log generation, or a few expensive queries), then exhaust the cheaper, reversible remedies: fixing query and index design, shortening transactions, eliminating unnecessary writes, batching, correcting connection behavior, managing data lifecycle, using vertical headroom, and separating workloads. Only when the single-instance write path is genuinely maxed after those steps does sharding become justified.
s1_definition.analogy: The main vault at National Bank of India is filling up and the staff want to build a second vault across town. That is a huge, permanent commitment — now every transaction has to know which vault holds which customer, and you can no longer move cash between two customers in one simple step. Before committing to that, the manager checks what is actually slow: is it one jammed door (a bad query), too many clerks fighting over one ledger (lock contention), not enough counters open (connections), or just an undersized vault that a bigger room would fix? Most of the time, fixing the jammed door or getting a bigger room solves it, and the second vault is never needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sharding permanently changes how your application is written, so first find the actual saturated resource and exhaust every cheaper, reversible fix before you shard.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sharding — horizontally partitioning data across multiple independent database instances — is the most expensive and least reversible scaling step, because it permanently changes how the application queries data: cross-shard joins, transactions, and unique constraints become hard or impossible, and every query must carry or derive a shard key. Before sharding you first diagnose which specific resource is actually saturated (CPU, lock contention, connection pressure, write-ahead-log generation, or a few expensive queries), then exhaust the cheaper, reversible remedies: fixing query and index design, shortening transactions, eliminating unnecessary writes, batching, correcting connection behavior, managing data lifecycle, using vertical headroom, and separating workloads. Only when the single-instance write path is genuinely maxed after those steps does sharding become justified.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The main vault at National Bank of India is filling up and the staff want to build a second vault across town. That is a huge, permanent commitment — now every transaction has to know which vault holds which customer, and you can no longer move cash between two customers in one simple step. Before committing to that, the manager checks what is actually slow: is it one jammed door (a bad query), too many clerks fighting over one ledger (lock contention), not enough counters open (connections), or just an undersized vault that a bigger room would fix? Most of the time, fixing the jammed door or getting a bigger room solves it, and the second vault is never needed.

**One line to remember:** Sharding permanently changes how your application is written, so first find the actual saturated resource and exhaust every cheaper, reversible fix before you shard.

sections.s2_technical:
The first step is diagnosis, because "approaching write capacity" is a symptom, not a cause, and each cause has a different cheap fix. I look at CPU utilisation, lock waits, the connection count versus the limit, the write-ahead-log generation rate, and the slowest queries. PostgreSQL exposes this directly: `pg_stat_activity` shows active queries and what they wait on, `pg_stat_statements` ranks queries by total time and calls, and WAL generation can be read from the server. Often the "write capacity" problem is actually one of these specific resources, and only one.

If it is a handful of expensive queries or missing indexes, the fix is query and index design. A write that triggers a full-table scan to check a constraint, or an update that touches more rows than necessary, consumes far more resource than it should. Adding the right index, or rewriting the query to touch fewer rows, can cut write cost dramatically. This is the cheapest and most common win.

If it is lock contention, the fix is shortening transactions and reducing hot rows. A long transaction holds locks and bloats the write path; splitting a long transaction, moving non-essential work outside it, and avoiding updating the same hot row from many sessions (for example by using append-only inserts or sharded counters within the same database) reduces contention without changing the deployment model.

If it is unnecessary writes, the fix is to stop writing what you do not need. Services often write audit rows, denormalised copies, or status updates far more often than required. Eliminating redundant writes, coalescing multiple updates into one, and using upserts instead of delete-then-insert all reduce the write rate directly.

If writes are many and small, batching helps enormously. Inserting a thousand rows in one batched statement generates far less overhead and WAL than a thousand single-row inserts, and committing less often (within durability limits) reduces the per-commit cost. The JDBC batch API and multi-row inserts are the tools here.

Connection behavior is a frequent hidden cause. Too many connections cause contention and memory pressure; a connection pool that is too large can make PostgreSQL slower, not faster. Putting a connection pooler like PgBouncer in front, and sizing pools to the database's real concurrency sweet spot, often recovers headroom that looked like a capacity wall.

Data lifecycle matters because a table that grows forever makes every write slower through index bloat and vacuum pressure. Archiving or partitioning old data by time, and deleting what is no longer needed, keeps the working set small and writes fast. Native table partitioning by range is a powerful middle step — it keeps one logical table but splits it physically, which speeds writes and maintenance without the application pain of sharding.

Vertical headroom is the simplest lever: a bigger instance with more CPU, memory, and faster disk can carry you a long way, and it is instant and reversible. It is often dismissed as "not real scaling," but for a write wall that is really an undersized instance, it is exactly the right fix and buys time.

Workload separation splits read and write pressure. Moving heavy reads and reporting to read replicas takes load off the primary, and moving an unrelated high-write workload into its own database removes contention. This is functional partitioning, which is far cheaper than sharding because each database still serves a coherent, self-contained workload.

The senior nuance is the ordering and the irreversibility argument. Sharding should be last because it changes application development permanently — you lose easy cross-shard transactions and joins, you must choose a shard key that you will be stuck with, and resharding later is painful. So I work through diagnosis, then query and index fixes, then transaction and write reduction, then batching and connection tuning, then data lifecycle and partitioning, then vertical scale and workload separation, and I only recommend sharding when the single primary is genuinely saturated on a fundamental resource after all of that, and the write rate is projected to keep growing beyond what one instance can ever serve.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the transaction-ledger database is "approaching write capacity" and an engineer proposes sharding by account id immediately.

Problem 1 — nobody has established what is actually saturated. A diagnosis shows the write rate is dominated by a flood of single-row inserts from the transaction logger, plus a long transaction that holds locks. This is exactly why diagnosis comes before any structural change.

Problem 2 — the single-row inserts are the biggest cost. Batching them into multi-row inserts cuts the write operations dramatically, recovering headroom without touching the deployment model. This is exactly the batching remedy.

Problem 3 — old ledger rows going back years are bloating the table and slowing every write. Partitioning the table by month keeps the hot partition small and fast. This is exactly the data-lifecycle remedy, and it is far cheaper than sharding.

The demo simulates the write path, measures write operations under naive single-row inserts versus batched inserts, applies a long-transaction fix, and shows the recovered capacity so that sharding is shown to be unnecessary for this workload.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a write workload of ten thousand ledger inserts per burst from the transaction logger, plus diagnostic readings of insert rate, lock waits, and connection usage.

Step 1: The diagnostics run first. With five thousand single-row inserts per second, low lock waits, and connections well under the limit, the diagnosis is write amplification from many small inserts — not a fundamental write-capacity wall and not something sharding is the right fix for.

Step 2: The naive write path writes each of the ten thousand rows as its own write operation, producing ten thousand operations, each a round-trip, a commit, and write-ahead-log generation. This is the load that looked like a capacity wall.

Step 3: The batching remedy groups the ten thousand rows into batches of five hundred, producing just twenty write operations instead of ten thousand. The same data is persisted, but the per-operation overhead and write-ahead-log volume drop by orders of magnitude.

Step 4: The demo reports the reduction — ten thousand operations down to twenty, a five-hundred-fold reduction in write operations. That recovered headroom is almost always enough to move the write path well back from its limit.

Step 5: The conclusion is that the write-capacity symptom was caused by write amplification, fixed cheaply and reversibly by batching, so sharding — which would have permanently complicated every query and transaction — is deferred, not undertaken.

```

2026-10-24 18:40:08 [INFO] Batched wrote 10000 rows in 20 ops
2026-10-24 18:40:08 [INFO] Write ops: naive=10000 batched=20 → 500x reduction
2026-10-24 18:40:08 [INFO] Headroom recovered WITHOUT sharding — sharding deferred
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When someone says PostgreSQL is approaching its write capacity and proposes sharding, my first point is that sharding is the most expensive and least reversible step available, so it must be last, not first. Sharding permanently changes how the application is written: cross-shard joins, transactions, and unique constraints become hard or impossible, every query has to carry or derive a shard key, and resharding later is painful. So before I would even discuss it, I insist on diagnosis and on exhausting the cheaper, reversible fixes.

Diagnosis comes first because "approaching write capacity" is a symptom, not a cause, and each cause has a different cheap remedy. I look at CPU, lock waits, connection count versus the limit, write-ahead-log generation rate, and the slowest queries, using pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements. Usually the problem turns out to be one specific resource — a handful of expensive queries, lock contention from long transactions, connection pressure, or write amplification from many tiny inserts — not a fundamental wall.

Then I work through the ladder. If it is expensive queries or missing indexes, I fix query and index design, which is the cheapest and most common win. If it is lock contention, I shorten transactions and reduce hot-row updates. If there are unnecessary writes, I eliminate or coalesce them. If writes are many and small, I batch them, which cuts round-trips and write-ahead-log volume dramatically — in the scenario I described, batching ten thousand single-row inserts into batches of five hundred turned ten thousand write operations into twenty, a five-hundred-fold reduction. I right-size connections with a pooler like PgBouncer, I manage data lifecycle by partitioning or archiving old data so the hot set stays small, I use vertical headroom because a bigger instance is instant and reversible, and I separate workloads by moving heavy reads to replicas and unrelated high-write workloads to their own database.

The reason the ordering matters so much is the irreversibility. Every step before sharding is reversible and local — I can add an index, batch writes, or bump instance size and roll it back if it does not help. Sharding is a one-way door that taxes every future query and every developer for the life of the system. So I only recommend it when the single primary is genuinely saturated on a fundamental resource after all the cheaper fixes, and the write rate is projected to keep growing beyond what one instance can ever serve.

In my banking work this exact situation came up with the transaction ledger. The team wanted to shard by account id, but diagnosis showed the load was dominated by single-row inserts from the transaction logger plus one long lock-holding transaction. Batching the inserts and shortening the transaction recovered so much headroom that the write path dropped well below its limit, and partitioning the ledger by month kept the hot partition fast as the table grew. We never needed to shard, and we avoided permanently complicating every query and transaction in the system. That is the heart of my answer: find the actual saturated resource, exhaust the cheap reversible fixes, and treat sharding as a last resort you take with your eyes open to its permanent cost.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
